summary:
Osmaniye province has no trans-specific ordinance, enforcement programme or local institution in the sourced material. A trans visitor to Osmaniye stands under the national framework of Türkiye, which applies here without local modification.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Türkiye since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender change has been available since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare homosexuality are assessed under a definition treating it as a 'psychosexual illness', must supply photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' being leaked publicly.

Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and most other cities in most years, deploying tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans. In June 2025 the authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans Pride marches; police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force and more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still continuing at year's end.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images on social media incompatible with 'society's moral values' and that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities.

Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an assault that would criminalise any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible to obtain; they were ultimately not submitted to parliament. In 2026 the draft judicial package's LGBTI-discriminatory provisions were removed. A February 2026 press report described a proposed law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison; it was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill (the 12th judicial package).

In June 2025 the Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency, part of the Ministry of Health, banned the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21.
tangentialFactors:
Legislative pressure on LGBTI expression has been episodic rather than settled: three draft packages surfaced in 2025 without reaching parliament, and the discriminatory provisions of the 2026 judicial package were stripped before adoption. A visitor reading only the enacted text would therefore see a less restrictive regime than the one officials have repeatedly tried to enact.

Pride bans since 2015 have been applied across multiple cities, not only Istanbul, so event-related policing risk is a national pattern rather than an Istanbul peculiarity.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change has been available in Türkiye since 1988, but the June 2025 Ministry of Health ban on prescribing and supplying gender-affirming hormones for people under 21 restricts access for younger residents.

Residents who are openly LGBTQ are barred from military service under a classification of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', with photographic proof required and a risk that the resulting 'unfit report' becomes public.

Associations organising for LGBTI rights face dissolution proceedings, as in the İzmir court's December 2025 order against the Young LGBTI+ Association, and no comprehensive anti-discrimination law protects sexual orientation or gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any of the three 2025 draft packages or the February 2026 proposal criminalising encouragement of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

The sources do not document Osmaniye-specific policing, facilities or healthcare access for trans visitors; the province-level picture rests on the absence of local instruments rather than on observed local practice.
